opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because I think there's often a gap between what the benchmark number says and what we actually want the model to be able to do. A benchmark is really a proxy. We pick some fixed set of examples, drawn from some distribution, and we say if you do well here, you've probably learned the underlying capability. But models are extremely good at finding whatever shortcut gets them the score, and that shortcut may or may not be the thing we care about.

So the first thing I look at is robustness to shifts that shouldn't matter. If a model has really learned the task, then small changes that a human would consider irrelevant, like rephrasing a question, changing the background of an image, or moving to a slightly different data source, shouldn't cause performance to collapse. When you see a big drop under those kinds of shifts, it's a strong signal that the model was relying on spurious correlations rather than the actual structure of the problem.

One interesting thing we've seen in our work is that in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance are often strongly correlated across models. They tend to fall on a line. That's useful because it tells you that a lot of the "gains" on a benchmark simply come along with a predictable gain out of distribution. They don't reflect any fundamentally new robustness. So the interesting question becomes whether a method moves you *off* that line, which would suggest something qualitatively different is going on, rather than just a better fit to the training distribution.

The second thing is contamination and memorization, which matters much more now with large pretrained models. When models are trained on huge swaths of the internet, it's really hard to know whether a benchmark example, or something very close to it, was seen during training. So high accuracy might reflect recall rather than reasoning. Constructing fresh evaluations, perturbing existing ones, or checking performance on problems that were created after the training cutoff can help separate those.

Third, I like to look beyond aggregate accuracy at the structure of the errors. If a model truly understands a task, its mistakes should look somewhat sensible. If it gets the hard cases right but fails on trivially easy variants, or if it's inconsistent, answering a question one way and a logically equivalent version another way, that tells you the competence is pretty brittle.

And finally, I think we have to be honest that "solved" is always relative to what we want to deploy the model for. A benchmark can be saturated while the real-world task is far from solved, because deployment brings distribution shift, adversarial users, long-tail inputs, and so on. So the way I'd frame it is that benchmark performance is necessary evidence but not sufficient. You need to stress-test the model in ways that probe whether it has captured the right underlying mechanism, not just the patterns that happen to work on that particular dataset.

r001.rationale: The response discusses fixed benchmark examples, shortcuts, and benchmark gains, but does not state that scaling compute on benchmark-like data can produce strong benchmark performance.

r002.rationale: The response says benchmark performance is necessary but not sufficient and explains that deployment shifts, adversarial users, and long-tail inputs can expose failures.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because benchmark performance is really just a proxy. What we actually care about is whether the model has learned the underlying capability, and a number on a test set doesn't tell you that on its own. So the way I think about it is: what would it mean to have solved the task, and does the benchmark actually certify that?

The first thing I ask is whether the evaluation distribution is really the distribution we care about. A lot of benchmarks are constructed in a very particular way, often from a single source, with annotation artifacts, with spurious correlations that a model can latch onto. And so a model can get very high accuracy by exploiting those shortcuts rather than doing the thing we intended. The classic examples are in natural language inference, where lexical overlap or the presence of a negation word was predictive of the label, and models were essentially solving a much easier problem than the one we thought we were posing.

So concretely, I like to look at robustness to distribution shift. If I take the same task but change the source, change the style, or introduce small perturbations that shouldn't matter semantically, does performance hold up? If the model is truly solving the task, those changes should be mostly irrelevant. If performance collapses, that tells you the benchmark number was measuring something narrower than the capability.

The second thing is contamination, which has become a much bigger deal with large pretrained models. If the test set, or something very close to it, appeared in pretraining, then high accuracy is partly memorization. And it's actually quite hard to rule that out, so I tend to treat results on older public benchmarks with some skepticism and put more weight on evaluations that were created after the model was trained, or that are generated procedurally so the exact instances couldn't have been seen.

And then the third piece, which I think is underappreciated, is understanding the failure modes rather than just the aggregate number. Two models can have identical average accuracy and have completely different error profiles. One might fail on rare but important subgroups, one might fail in ways that are correlated with each other. So I'd rather see a breakdown, stress tests, adversarial probes, and ideally some notion of whether the model knows when it's wrong, than a single leaderboard score.

So to put it together: I don't think any one benchmark result establishes that a task is solved. What convinces me is a consistent pattern across shifted distributions, fresh or held-out data, and targeted probes of the mechanisms I'd expect a real solution to rely on. Benchmarks are useful for tracking progress and comparing methods, but the moment we start optimizing directly for them, they stop being good measures of the thing we care about. That's sort of the core tension.

r001.rationale: The response discusses high benchmark accuracy from shortcuts and contamination, but does not state that scaling compute on benchmark-like data can produce that performance.

r002.rationale: It questions whether benchmark scores show the underlying capability and says performance may collapse when the task is evaluated on shifted sources, styles, or meaning-preserving perturbations.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to ask what we mean by “solved.” A benchmark tells us how well a model performs on a particular distribution of examples. That’s useful, but the task we have in mind is often broader than what those examples capture.

For instance, a model might get very high accuracy by using a feature that happens to correlate with the label in the benchmark. If that correlation changes, the model can fail even though, from our perspective, the task hasn’t changed at all. So I’d want to test what happens when we vary things that should be irrelevant to the answer, or evaluate in a different setting where we still expect the same capability to work.

And then it’s important to look at the failures, rather than just the average score. Are there systematic groups of examples where it struggles? Does a small change cause a prediction to flip? Those tests help us understand what the model has actually learned. Strong benchmark performance is evidence of progress, but saying we’ve solved the task requires being explicit about the conditions under which we expect the model to succeed.

r002.rationale: It questions whether benchmark scores mean the task is solved and explains that testing in a different setting or after small changes can reveal failures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing to ask is what we mean by “solved.” A benchmark gives us a particular distribution of examples, and strong performance tells us that the model does well on that distribution. But the task we care about is usually broader than that.

For example, is the model using information that’s actually relevant to the task, or is there some correlation in the dataset that lets it get the right answer? Those can look identical if you only look at average test accuracy. One way to distinguish them is to change that correlation while keeping the underlying task the same and see whether performance holds up.

So I’d want to look at how the model behaves under those changes, where it fails, and whether those failures matter for the intended application. A high benchmark score is useful evidence, but the strength of the conclusion depends on what the benchmark actually tests.

r001.rationale: The response says strong performance reflects doing well on a benchmark’s example distribution, but it does not mention scaling compute or training on benchmark-like data.

r002.rationale: It proposes changing a dataset correlation while keeping the underlying task the same, then checking performance and failures relevant to the intended application.
